{"translation_en":"“Bring her to me!” said her mother, rushing forward to embrace her. “How **I love you**, my poor child! How I love you!”","larger_context_summary":"Emma Bovary addresses her young daughter, Berthe, in a sudden display of maternal tenderness. The scene belongs to the period in which Emma’s involvement with Rodolphe is drawing her away from domestic life; recollection of her father and childhood has briefly reawakened feelings of family attachment, nostalgia, and guilt. Calling Berthe “my poor child,” Emma rushes to embrace her and repeats the declaration, making this an emotionally charged moment of attempted reconnection rather than a settled change in Emma’s conduct or in their relationship.","interpretive_commentary":"The wording directly predicates love of the child, so its central force is a strong, truth-conditional avowal. The degree construction “How I love you,” immediate repetition, exclamation marks, and bodily rush toward Berthe make the expression feel affectively discharged rather than merely informative. That supports expressive force, though intensity alone does not prove that the words are wholly spontaneous or unreflective; the scene can also be read as Emma consciously yielding to a temporary surge of maternal feeling. Her embrace may briefly affect the relationship, but neither the gesture nor the declaration performs an undertaking, promise, or change of status. The broader instability of Emma’s domestic attachments does not by itself make the statement deceptive: it may sincerely articulate a powerful feeling at this particular moment without guaranteeing durable maternal conduct."}
